issues.legal_issue: A High Court may not overturn concurrent factual findings in a second appeal by reappreciating evidence unless a substantial question of law arises and the findings meet a recognized basis for interference.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court gave reasons based on the evidence and both dismissed the title suit.
The High Court framed a question concerning ownership and possession that the Supreme Court held was not a substantial question of law.
The High Court reappreciated the evidence and set aside the concurrent findings.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction in the second appeal; its judgment was set aside and the judgments dismissing the suit were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as amended in 1976, a substantial question of law is a prerequisite to second-appeal jurisdiction. A High Court cannot substitute its view for that of the first appellate court unless the findings are contrary to mandatory law or Supreme Court precedent, or rest on inadmissible evidence or no evidence. Interference may also be justified where material evidence was omitted or inadmissible evidence was relied upon. The Court relied on Kondiba Dagadu Kadam v. Savitribai Sopan Gujar and Ishwar Dass Jain v. Sohan Lal.

rule.if: second_appeal and concurrent_reasoned_factual_findings and high_court_reappreciates_evidence and not qualifying_basis_for_interference

predicates.second_appeal: The challenged decision was made by a High Court hearing a second appeal.
predicates.concurrent_reasoned_factual_findings: The trial court and first appellate court reached the same factual conclusions for reasons based on the evidence.
predicates.high_court_reappreciates_evidence: The High Court reassessed the evidence and substituted its factual conclusions for those of the lower courts.
predicates.qualifying_basis_for_interference: The findings were contrary to mandatory law or controlling precedent, rested on inadmissible or no evidence, or resulted from omission of material evidence.

issues.definition: When a High Court reexamines evidence and overturns concurrent, reasoned factual findings in a second appeal without a qualifying basis for interference, it has no authority to do so.

issues.legal_issue: A defendant resisting a title claim based on a sale deed may contend that the deed is fictitious, collusive, nominal, not acted upon, or not binding on the defendant without first bringing a separate proceeding to set it aside.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a declaration of ownership based on registered sale deeds.
The person whose interest was said to be affected by the earlier sale deed had not signed it.
The defendants contended that the earlier deed was nominal and not acted upon, and that it did not bind them.
The defendants had not brought separate proceedings to set aside the deeds.
issues.conclusion: The defendants could raise those defences in the title suit without independently challenging the sale deed by a separate suit or counterclaim.
issues.legal_principle: A defendant may raise any legitimate plea available in law to defeat the plaintiff’s claim, including that a deed relied upon to establish title is void, fictitious, collusive, nominal, not intended to be acted upon, or not binding on the defendant. The Court relied on Vidhyadhar v. Manikrao and Another.

predicates.declaration_suit_based_on_sale_deed: The plaintiff sought a declaration of ownership based on a sale deed.
predicates.defendant_not_bound_by_deed: The defendant was not a party to, or otherwise bound by, the deed relied upon by the plaintiff.
predicates.defendant_disputes_deed_as_not_genuine_o: The defendant contended that the deed was not genuine, was not intended to operate, or did not bind the defendant.

issues.definition: In a suit for title based on a deed, a defendant who disputes being bound by it may raise a legitimate challenge to the deed as a defence without a separate proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: An unregistered written record of an oral family partition may be considered as a list corroborating the arrangement and the parties’ conduct when it records an arrangement already made orally rather than itself creating or extinguishing rights.
material_facts: The plaintiff admitted that an oral partition had taken place and that he received a share consistent with the written record.
The written record was signed by the plaintiff and other family members and by people associated with the village council.
Witnesses supported the execution of the record.
The lower courts treated the document as admissible, while the High Court excluded it solely because it was unregistered.
issues.conclusion: The document could be considered as a list of properties partitioned and as corroborative evidence of the oral arrangement and the parties’ conduct; the High Court erred in excluding it solely for want of registration.
issues.legal_principle: A writing that merely records a completed oral family arrangement does not require registration as an instrument creating or extinguishing rights, and an unregistered written family arrangement may be used as corroborative evidence explaining the arrangement and the parties’ conduct. A family settlement may also operate as an estoppel between its participants. The Court relied on Kale v. Deputy Director of Consolidation, S. Shanmugam Pillai v. K. Shanmugam Pillai, and Subraya M.N. v. Vittala M.N. and Others.

rule.if: family_partition_proceeding and prior_oral_partition_admitted and writing_records_existing_arrangement and participants_signed_or_followed_arrangement

predicates.family_partition_proceeding: The dispute concerns an alleged partition or family arrangement among family members.
predicates.prior_oral_partition_admitted: A participant admitted that the family arrangement had already been made orally.
predicates.writing_records_existing_arrangement: The writing records or lists the terms or property allotments of the existing arrangement rather than itself creating or extinguishing rights.
predicates.participants_signed_or_followed_arrangem: The participants signed the writing or their conduct was consistent with the recorded arrangement.

issues.definition: When participants admit an oral family arrangement and the writing records that existing arrangement, the writing may corroborate the arrangement and the participants’ conduct even if it is unregistered.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant does not establish ownership merely by relying on registered sale deeds where the earlier deed was not binding on a joint-family interest holder and was not acted upon, and the later deed was found to be sham.
material_facts: The property had been purchased by a family member and was later treated as joint-family property.
The earlier sale deed was signed by some family members but not by the family member whose interest was asserted by the defendants.

The evidence supported findings that the earlier deed was not acted upon, including that the purchaser’s name was not recorded in the revenue records during the relevant period and that the plaintiff was uncertain about the consideration.
The plaintiff admitted that there had been no partition when the earlier deed was made.
The lower courts found the later sale deed to be sham, including because the evidence about its consideration was inconsistent.
issues.conclusion: The sale deeds did not establish the plaintiff’s title on the evidence in this case, and the suit for a declaration of ownership was properly dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held on the evidence that the earlier sale deed could not bind a family member who had not signed it, where the property was joint-family property and the transaction was not acted upon. It also upheld the finding that the subsequent deed was sham. A defendant who is a stranger to a deed may contest whether it was intended to operate or bind the defendant, as recognized in Vidhyadhar v. Manikrao and Another.

rule.if: declaration_suit_based_on_chain_of_sales and joint_family_property and affected_family_member_did_not_sign_earlier_transfer and earlier_transfer_not_acted_upon and later_transfer_found_sham

predicates.declaration_suit_based_on_chain_of_sales: The plaintiff sought a declaration of ownership based on a sequence of sale deeds.
predicates.joint_family_property: The property was held or treated as joint-family property when the earlier transfer was made.
predicates.affected_family_member_did_not_sign_earl: The family member whose interest was asserted did not sign the earlier transfer.
predicates.earlier_transfer_not_acted_upon: The evidence showed that the earlier transfer was not acted upon by the parties.
predicates.later_transfer_found_sham: The evidence supported a finding that a later transfer in the plaintiff’s chain of title was sham.

issues.definition: A claimant relying on successive sales does not establish title when the earlier transfer of joint-family property did not bind an affected family member and was not acted upon, and the later transfer was sham.
